title: The broken dam
hookLine: the people of Sheba are given two gardens, turn away, and the dam bursts (34:15–17)

cards: Nobody thanks a light switch. A gift that works every day goes invisible. Surah thirty-four carries the name of a people, Saba', Sheba, whose gift was water, held back and shared out across their fields.
Near Ma'rib in Yemen, old stone ruins of a dam still stand, and commentators connect them with this story. The surah tells it in three short verses, and it isn't really about engineering at all.

teach.h: TWO GARDENS: EAT, AND GIVE THANKS.
teach.b: Verse fifteen. There was a sign for Sheba in their homeland: two gardens, one on the right and one on the left. The instruction that came with them is short.
Pickthall: "Eat of the provision of your Lord and render thanks to Him. A fair land and an indulgent Lord!" That last line is almost a postcard: a good land, and a Lord who forgives.
Verse sixteen: but they turned away.

So Allah sent on them sayl al-'arim, the flood of the dam, or as some translate it, the overwhelming flood. Their two gardens were exchanged for gardens of bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a few lote trees.
Verse seventeen gives the reason in one word: kafaru, they were ungrateful. Classical dictionaries connect the root, k-f-r, with covering over.
Ingratitude covers a gift, like soil over a seed, until you stop seeing it. The Qur'an doesn't list a dramatic crime. Nobody told them to do anything hard.

Eat, and give thanks: that was the whole instruction, and it was the thanks they let go. Commentators connect the burst dam with the dam at Ma'rib; the Qur'an itself doesn't give a date or name the dam.
It names the pattern: a gift received without gratitude starts to come apart, and what replaces it is thin and bitter.
A few verses earlier, about Dawud's family, the same surah says it plainly: few of Allah's servants are thankful.

how: Many Muslims say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after, and scholars often cite the story of Sheba when teaching that gratitude (shukr) preserves blessings.

o: a garden in paradise, promised to the thankful
a people given two gardens, who stopped giving thanks
a desert queen's palace, made of polished glass

p: one on the right, one on the left

s: the Qur'an names Sheba's dam and dates its collapse
it names neither; commentators link it to the Ma'rib dam.
Sheba's instruction was simply to eat and give thanks
verse fifteen: eat of your Lord's provision and render thanks to Him.
their gardens became tamarisk and bitter fruit

games.q: you live in Sheba. two gardens, a fair land, a forgiving Lord. you're asked only to eat and give thanks. what did Sheba do?
o: gave thanks, and kept the gardens.
games.why: they turned away, and the flood of the dam came. the Qur'an's one word for why is ingratitude.

practice: If you can, pour a glass of water and hold it, and think about where it came from: rain, a river, a reservoir, a pipe someone laid. Take a slow sip.
If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah, the praise belongs to God, as many Muslims do after drinking; if not, simply notice the gift in your hand.

wordCard.voice: Sheba, the people with two gardens and every provision, whose own ingratitude brought the flood that broke their dam. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the flood of al-'arim, often read as the dam, or the overwhelming flood.
